## Overview {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## Questions this lesson answers

- How do you find a gene in Ensembl and read its Gene tab?
- What is the difference between all annotated transcripts, protein-coding transcripts, and the MANE Select transcript?
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Search Ensembl by gene name.
2. Choose an appropriate transcript for downstream work, and justify the choice.
3. Turn browser tracks on and off, and explore transcript information.
:::

| | |
|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | ~1.5 hours (5 exercises, roughly 15 to 20 minutes each) |
| **Level** | Introductory |
| **Prerequisites** | Genes, transcripts, exons, UTRs, and the idea of a reference genome |
| **Software needed** | A web browser only |

: Practical details {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

::: {.callout-caution title="Ensembl updates" collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
Ensembl publishes a new release several times a year, and annotation changes
between releases. Transcript counts, transcript names, identifier versions, and
even the set of associated phenotypes may differ from the answers given here.
Treat any mismatch as a discussion point rather than a mistake: look at
which release you are looking at.
:::

## Learning the Ensembl data platform {#sec-ensembl}

Before using Ensembl, you should become familiar with its interface and the types of data it provides.

Start by **completing the [introductory tutorial on the Ensembl data platform](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/ensembl-data-platform/)**.

Take your time and make sure you understand the main concepts and how to navigate 
the platform before moving to the next step.


## Exploring the PCSK9 gene in human {#sec-pcsk9}

`PCSK9` encodes the proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.

### Locating the gene {#sec-pcsk9-locate}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🔬 Hands on

1. Go to <https://www.ensembl.org>.
2. Click the `Genome selector`, type **Human** in the search box, and click `Find`. 
3. Select the `Reference` genome, and click the green `Add` button.
4. Type **PCSK9** in the `Find a feature in the selected genomes` search box, and click `Find.`
5. Click the **PCSK9** gene in the results and choose to `View in Genome browser`.
6. Expand the side tab (top blue arrow) to view more information related to the **PCSK9** gene: `Genomic`, `Variation`, and `Regulation.` Notice the `Eye icon` that toggles the **View/Hide** function for each track.
7. Explore the genome browser view. Notice that to obtain more information you can **click the transcript** or the `...`, and you can also use the `Feature explorer` to find more information related to the `Transcripts` and the full `Transcript table` (among other info to be explored in the next class).  
:::

:::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## ❓ Question

1. Which chromosome and which strand is the gene on?
2. How many transcripts (splice variants) are annotated?   
3. How many transcripts are protein coding?
4. Which is the longest protein-coding transcript (exon length in bp), and how long is the protein it encodes (amino acid length)?
5. Which transcript would you take forward for further study, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Show answer"}
1. Chromosome 1, on the forward strand.
2. 16 transcripts.
3. 7 transcripts are protein coding.
4. The longest transcript is **ENST00000713786.2** with **3,852 bp**, coding for a **733 aa** protein.
5. **ENST00000302118.5** because it is the **MANE Select** transcript. MANE Select transcripts are agreed between **Ensembl** and **RefSeq** (two large databases) as the single representative transcript for a gene, with matching sequences in both databases, which makes results easier to compare across resources. Click on the `?` next to the MANE Select transcript for the formal definition.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Why "longest" and "best" are not the same thing

Note that the longest protein-coding transcript is not the one we choose to work with. Length is a poor proxy for biological relevance. 
Ask yourself: What would you do if a gene had no MANE Select transcript, and what
evidence would look for instead: Expression support, protein evidence,
**TSL** and **APPRIS** flags in the transcript table (click on the tags to learn more about them), publications, external databases?
:::
